events.text: Day 1 begins.

Good morning, everyone. Day one, so we're all working off nothing but gut reads and first impressions. I want to lay out how I'm thinking about this before we get to votes. With two mafia among nine, the biggest risk today is burning a lynch on the wrong person based on noise — someone being quiet isn't automatically suspicious, and someone being loud isn't automatically cleared. I'd rather we all share concrete observations: who's dodging questions, who's pushing hard for a quick vote without giving reasons, who's trying to blend in by being agreeable. I'll be paying attention to how people respond under direct pressure more than anything else today. For my own part, I have no strong read yet, and I'm not going to invent one just to look busy. I'd like to hear from a few of you before I commit to anything. Zara, you were on my mind because you haven't said much yet — what's your read on the group so far, and is there anyone you'd be comfortable voting for today or would you rather we hold?

Answering Theo directly since he asked me first.

My honest read: I have none yet, and I'd rather say that than manufacture a confident-sounding accusation off a single speech. Theo laid out a good frame — two mafia among nine, and the real danger today is a lynch on noise. I agree that quiet isn't guilt and loud isn't innocence, and I also want to add one thing to his list: watch for people who answer questions with process instead of content. "Let's hear from everyone first," "I don't want to rush," "we should build consensus" — that can be genuine, but it can also be a way to avoid saying anything falsifiable.

On my own vote: I would rather not cast a meaningful vote today than cast a random one. An abstention costs me nothing structurally, and a wrong vote costs the town a body. If I'm forced to name someone on the ballot, my vote goes to whoever refuses to answer a direct question when asked — not to whoever speaks the most or least.

So concretely: I have no accusation to make right now. I have no evidence, and I'm not going to pretend a hunch is evidence.

Theo, since you're the only one who's laid out reasoning so far, I do want to press you on one specific point: you said you'd be paying attention to how people respond under direct pressure. Does that mean you're naming a target today, or are you genuinely withholding until you have something? I want to know whether we're voting on a read or voting on a principle, because those turn out differently.

Zara, fair question, and I'll answer it straight: I'm withholding for now. I don't have a read I'd defend, and I'd rather be the person who says so on day one than the person who manufactures a target to look decisive. So we're voting on a principle today, not a read — unless someone gives us a real read between now and the ballot.

That said, your answer actually sharpened something for me. You said your vote goes to whoever refuses to answer a direct question. That's a falsifiable commitment, and I like that — it means if we end the day with a name on the ballot, you've told us in advance the standard you'll apply. I'll hold you to it, and I'll hold myself to the same standard.

But I want to press one specific point from your message, because it cuts both ways. You described process-answers as a potential evasion tactic, then your own answer was mostly framework: what you won't do, what you'd rather do, what costs what. The one concrete thing you offered was a conditional — vote for the non-answerer. Fine. But by that logic, the person most likely to receive your vote is whoever stays quiet longest today, which means mafia players who understand this dynamic can simply talk more and dodge nothing. So my question back to you is specific: if everyone at this table answers every question asked of them, and we still have no reads, does your vote default to abstention, or does it default to the person who spoke the most while saying the least? I think that distinction matters, because 'most words, least content' is exactly the profile you flagged, and I'd like to know whether you actually intend to apply it.

To the rest of the table: I'm not going to name a target just to fill silence. If you have an actual observation — something someone said or didn't say — put it on the record now. Vague vibes won't move me, but specifics will.

Felix, you and Kenji have both been quiet so far, and I don't want to assume that means anything. Felix, direct question: is there anyone here you'd currently vote for, and if not, what would someone have to do today to earn your suspicion? I'm asking because your answer tells us whether you're actually tracking the game or waiting to see which way the wind blows before committing.

Theo, straight answer: I don't currently have a vote I'd defend, so I'd abstain if the ballot were now. Quietness alone won't earn my suspicion; neither will loudness clear anyone. What would earn it is a direct question being dodged, a stated standard being applied selectively, or a push for a lynch without concrete reasons. Zara's "vote the non-answerer" standard is at least falsifiable, and I don't scumread her for it, though Theo's loophole point is fair: it can be gamed by talking more while saying nothing. I'm watching whether people actually apply the standards they announce.

Kenji, Theo grouped you and me as quiet, and I can only answer for myself. So I want a concrete response from you, not a vibe: is there anyone you'd currently vote for, and if so, which specific statement or behavior would you cite? If not, what exact thing today would flip your vote? I'm yielding to you for that answer.

Felix, to answer you directly: no, there is no one I would vote for right now. We have had four speeches, and so far the entire discussion between Theo, Zara, and you has been an exchange of abstract philosophies—agreeing not to lynch on noise, debating whether process answers or non-answers are scummy, and establishing that nobody has reads yet. Voting someone on that would be purely arbitrary.

What would flip my vote today comes down to three concrete behaviors:
1. Parroting without substance: someone entering the discussion simply endorsing the prevailing "be careful, look for dodgers" framework without offering any distinct perspective or friction of their own, using consensus as camouflage.
2. Opportunistic wagoning: if a name starts gaining traction later in the day and someone glides onto that vote with shallow, borrowed justification rather than independent reasons.
3. Deflection or selective answering: if someone is pressed on a specific contradiction and responds by talking around it, changing the subject, or retreating into vague process generalities.

More importantly, we are several speeches in and over half the table—Arjun, Omar, Lucia, Sam, and Elena—has not been heard from. Repeating to each other that we have no reads isn't going to generate reads; we need to see how the rest of the players engage and where the natural friction develops. I am leaving this open to the poll so those who want to enter the conversation can do so directly.

Zara, I disagree that abstaining costs town nothing structurally. It can mean giving up a chance to eliminate mafia and forfeiting potentially useful voting information, while a night kill may still follow. That doesn't make a weak lynch automatically better, but it makes the choice a tradeoff.

I'm not ready to vote for anyone yet. I do think your stated preference deserves scrutiny: what kind of evidence, short of someone refusing a direct question, would make you support a vote today?

Omar, direct answer, and I'll make it a commitment rather than a principle, since you're right that "abstain, costs nothing" is lazy.

Here is my updated standard for today, in writing, before the ballot. My vote goes to a player only if one of these is true:
1. They refused or visibly dodged a direct question asked of them.
2. Their own stated standard was contradicted by their own behavior within this discussion — the "everyone else is doing X, but I don't" problem.
3. They made a checkable claim about the content of another player's speech that the record contradicts.

If none of those three applies to anyone, I abstain. Yes, that risks forfeiting an elimination chance, but I want to correct my earlier framing: abstention does cost us, and specifically it costs us the information in who is willing to commit under pressure. That is a real cost and I'll accept it. What it doesn't cost is a town body, and I won't trade a body for a coin flip.

Theo, your loophole point was correct and I won't pretend otherwise: "vote the non-answerer" alone is gameable by talking more while saying nothing. Criterion 3 is my fix for that, and I'd note it also punishes the person who speaks confidently about someone else's speech without having listened. Theo, your framework discussion and your press on Felix and Kenji are consistent with what you've announced, so you're not where I look.

To the table generally: my standard is now falsifiable and narrow. Apply it to me. If I dodge a question, vote me.

Sam, you're the one person I have not heard from at all, and I'm going to ask you something specific rather than a general invitation. Two parts. First, name one concrete observation about a specific player here — something they said or failed to say — and tell me why it matters. Second, give me the name you would put on a ballot today and the single reason you'd defend it. If the honest answer is "I have no read and nothing would flip me yet," say exactly that, and tell me what specific thing would flip you. I'd rather hear a clean "no read" from you than a manufactured accusation, and I'd rather hear the reason behind your name than the name itself. I'm yielding to you for that.

Zara, one concrete observation: you said I was the one person you hadn't heard from, but Arjun, Lucia and Elena also hadn't spoken in the record. That matters because it shows how an inaccurate summary can happen without necessarily indicating mafia intent.

I have no vote I'd defend right now. A specific thing that could change that is someone misrepresenting another player's words after being corrected, then using that misrepresentation to push a vote. A simple mistake alone wouldn't be enough for me.

I also agree with Omar that abstaining has a cost: we lose a chance to eliminate mafia, and votes can give us information later. That doesn't make a random accusation worthwhile.

Zara, your third criterion would permit a vote for a checkably incorrect claim about another speech. How would you distinguish an honest mistake from a suspicious misrepresentation before voting on it?

Sam, you're right, and I want to correct myself before anything else: my claim that you were the only player I hadn't heard from was wrong. Arjun, Lucia and Elena have not spoken either. I stated that as fact and it wasn't, and I'd rather own it in the record than have it sit there as something people might build a case on. I don't read that as mafia evidence, and I don't read your correction as a play — you corrected a factual error without using it to push anyone. That's exactly the behavior I'd want to see.

To answer your question directly: how do I distinguish an honest mistake from a suspicious misrepresentation before voting on it? My threshold has three conditions, and all three must hold:
1. The claim is checkable against the record. If it isn't checkable, no vote, regardless of intent.
2. The claim was corrected in the record and the speaker continued to act on, or repeat, the bad version afterward. An honest mistake ends the moment it's corrected; a misrepresentation is what survives the correction.
3. The claim is being used to move a vote rather than merely to describe the discussion.

Now I'll apply that to myself and to the record, since a standard I won't apply to my own error isn't a standard.

On my error: condition 1 fails. It wasn't checkable-against-record in a way that implicates intent, and condition 3 fails because nobody pushed a vote on it. So no vote, and I accept the correction.

On someone else: Felix, in your message you wrote "Theo grouped you and me as quiet." Theo actually named Felix and Kenji as the quiet ones he was pressing. That is a checkable claim contradicted by the record, and I'm putting it on the table rather than burying it — but by my own conditions it fails #2 and #3, because it wasn't corrected and pressed further, and you were answering a question rather than using it to push a vote. So I'm not voting you on it. I'm asking for it on the record so the table can see whether it was a slip or something else, and I'd rather have your own words on it than my inference.

Felix, direct question: what exactly did Theo say he was grouping as quiet — "Felix and Kenji," or "Zara and Felix"? And separately, what would you have said if you'd noticed the discrepancy before answering?

Zara, direct answer: Theo said he was grouping "Felix and Kenji" as quiet. My line was addressed to Kenji — "Theo grouped you and me as quiet" — so "you and me" meant Kenji and me, Felix. It was not "Zara and Felix." I don't see a contradiction in the record; it's a pronoun-reference issue, not a checkable claim against Theo's words. If I'd noticed any discrepancy before answering, I would have said exactly that: Theo named Kenji and me, and I was answering as one of the two he named. I appreciate you putting it on the record, and I'd ask that the correction be noted plainly rather than treated as a live inconsistency. On my vote: I still have no defensible vote today. I won't vote Zara over what looks like an honest parsing error, and I won't manufacture a target to look decisive. My standard is the same as before: I'll vote someone if they dodge a direct question, apply a stated standard selectively after correction, or keep pushing a checkable misstatement after it's been corrected. Right now I see no one meeting that bar, so I would abstain if the ballot were immediate.

This is my first time speaking, so let me enter properly rather than as a name on Zara's list of the unheard.

First, a few record-keeping points. Zara's correction of her own error was handled the right way: she owned it immediately, didn't blame the record, and then applied her own criteria to herself and acknowledged the vote failed. That is the behavior she asked us to hold her to, and she held herself to it. I don't read Sam's correction as a gotcha either — he flagged the factual error without pushing a vote on it, which is exactly what a town player does with a small discrepancy. The Felix pronoun dispute resolved cleanly too: Theo named Felix and Kenji, Felix's "you and me" referred to Kenji and himself, and there was no checkable contradiction. I'd like that thread closed rather than kept warm.

Second, on the abstention debate between Omar and Zara: I lean toward Omar's framing. Zara's updated three criteria are narrow and falsifiable, and I respect that, but I agree that a day where everyone meets her standard and nobody gets voted is a day where mafia learn how we all think while we learn nothing about them. I'm not saying lynch someone random — I'm saying that if we reach the ballot with genuinely nothing, a no-elimination day is a real cost, not a neutral outcome, and we should feel that cost when we choose it.

Third, what I'm actually watching today. With two mafia among nine, the most useful information right now is behavioral: who answers direct questions cleanly, who corrects their own errors, who pushes votes without reasons. So far the people who've spoken have mostly done well on that — Theo committed to withholding rather than manufacturing a target, Felix gave a concrete standard, Kenji listed specific flip conditions. Nobody has yet done anything that trips Zara's criteria as far as I can tell. That's genuinely no reads, not lazy no reads.

What concerns me more is that Arjun, Lucia, and I were silent for most of this discussion, and the quiet pool is where a mafia player most comfortably hides on day one. I can't read myself usefully, but I can say my silence was absence, not strategy, and I have no accusation to make right now.

Arjun, since you're the only other player who hasn't entered the discussion yet, I have a direct question with two parts, same structure Zara gave Sam: first, name one concrete observation about a specific player's behavior so far — something they said or failed to say — and why it matters to you. Second, tell me whether you'd vote today, abstain, or hold, and what specifically would move you off that position. If your honest answer is that you have nothing, say that plainly — I'd rather hear a clean no-read than a manufactured one. I'm yielding to you for that answer.

Elena, answering your two-part question directly.

One concrete observation: Zara has been the loudest architect of standards all day, and she built three of them after her first framework was successfully challenged on the non-answerer loophole. That's not inherently suspicious — updating under pressure is what I'd want to see — but it does mean the most discussed standard in the game came from the player who was also corrected for a factual error earlier. I'm not scumreading her for either, but I want to note that Zara has shaped more of the conversation's direction than anyone else today, and that's worth tracking regardless of alignment.

On my position: I would abstain if the ballot were now. Nobody has met any of the three criteria Zara laid out — no one has dodged a direct question, no one has contradicted their own stated standard in a way that survives correction, and the checkable-claim criterion hasn't been triggered either. Felix's pronoun issue resolved cleanly, Zara's self-correction was honest, and the rest has been framework debate.

What would move me: someone pressing a specific contradiction after it's been corrected, or a sudden convergence on a name without independent reasons — exactly the opportunistic wagoning Kenji flagged. If that happens, I'll engage.

One thing I'll add that nobody has raised: we've spent most of this day on meta-discussion about how to read each other rather than on actual content. That's partly a function of having nothing yet, but it also means we're all performing credibility rather than testing it. The quiet pool — Lucia and I — hasn't been pressured much beyond Elena's question to me now. I'd rather have that pressure than avoid it.

Lucia here. I've been reading closely rather than hiding, and I'm not going to pretend I have a strong read yet. Zara has done a lot of the framing today. Her three criteria sound narrow, but criterion 1 depends entirely on what counts as checkable, and that gives the voter a lot of room. I'd like to see that test applied to someone other than Zara before we treat it as settled. Elena's point that the quiet pool is where mafia hide is fair, and I agree that silence shouldn't become a free pass. I also don't want us lynching over a pronoun dispute that Felix and Sam have already cleared up. Omar is right that abstaining costs us information, but a no-elimination day isn't automatically a loss either. I'm not voting anyone today. Kenji, you listed opportunistic wagoning as one of your flip conditions. Which specific current speech would you point to as a shallow bandwagon? Name the speech so we can test it against the record.

Lucia, to answer you directly: there is no such speech, because no wagon has formed.

When I laid out that criterion in my previous speech, it was explicitly prospective: 'if a name starts gaining traction later in the day and someone glides onto that vote with shallow, borrowed justification.' I was defining what would cause me to reconsider my stance in the future, not claiming an active bandwagon was already on the board. Every single player who has spoken so far—Theo, Zara, Felix, Omar, Sam, Elena, Arjun, and yourself—has explicitly declined to name a target and stated they would withhold or abstain. You cannot point to an opportunistic bandwagon when there is not even a single vote in play.

Your question treats a future trigger condition as if it were an active accusation against someone. That is either an honest misreading of my words or a test to see if I would manufacture a case to defend the statement. If it was a misreading, the record is now clear: no such speech exists, and I never claimed one did.

Lucia, to resolve this directly: did you genuinely interpret my statement as referring to an existing speech on the record, or what prompted you to ask for a specific speech when no votes have been cast?

Kenji, fair point, and I'll answer directly. I asked for a specific speech because your list named a behavior as a flip condition, and I wanted to test that criterion against the record before accepting it. I didn't mean to suggest you had already accused anyone, and I accept that the record shows no active wagon. My concern is narrower: 'shallow, borrowed justification' is a judgment call. Does agreeing with another player's reasons count as borrowed, or does it only count when the reasons are repeated without any independent check? I'm yielding to you for that answer, because the usefulness of your criterion depends on where that line sits. I still have no vote today. I'll abstain unless someone meets one of the criteria on the record.

Lucia, to answer your question directly: it is firmly the latter.

Agreeing with sound logic or building upon another player's observation is standard town collaboration. What makes a justification "shallow and borrowed" is when a player glides onto a developing wagon by parroting conclusions without showing any independent evaluation, testing, or nuance of their own—effectively using someone else's case as a shield to cast a vote while avoiding accountability for the push. If someone simply echoes another player's accusations right when momentum forms, without demonstrating that they actually examined the record or weighed the defense, that is what raises suspicion.

As this is my third and final speaking turn for Day 1, I want to clearly state my position heading into the vote. Every player has now entered the discussion. Across the board, people have answered direct inquiries, clarified misstatements when challenged, and refrained from forcing arbitrary targets. While Omar, Sam, and Elena correctly noted the structural tradeoffs and lost information of a no-elimination day, manufacturing a lynch out of thin air carries a much higher likelihood of hitting town than catching mafia.

Since no player has tripped any of the concrete behavioral criteria laid out today, my vote on the ballot will be an abstention. I am not yielding, allowing the poll to determine next steps for the table.

Since everyone has now entered the discussion, I want to use my turn to do two things: state where I stand for the ballot, and put one unresolved question on the record rather than let the day close on pure consensus.

First, my position. I still have no defensible vote. I've now watched every player speak, and the honest summary is that nobody has dodged a direct question, nobody has pushed a vote without reasons, and the two errors that surfaced — Zara's miscount of who hadn't spoken, and the Felix pronoun dispute — were both corrected cleanly and without being weaponized. By the standards this table has collectively built today, no one qualifies for my vote. I'll be abstaining unless something changes in the remaining turns, and I accept Omar and Sam's point that this costs us information. I'd rather pay that cost on day one with nine players alive than flip a coin on a body.

Second, the observation I want on the record. The most discussed commitment of the day belongs to Theo. He framed the day's approach, pressed Zara, Felix, and Kenji with specific questions, and told Zara he would hold both of them to the standard of voting the non-answerer. But that standard has since been replaced — Zara published three narrow criteria, and the table largely organized itself around them. Theo never said whether he accepts the updated version, whether his own behavior under it differs from his behavior under the original one, and most concretely: he said he'd apply the standard to himself, so he should say now whether anyone has met it in his view. If the answer is no, fine — that's a clean abstention with reasons. If the answer is yes and he's been sitting on a name all day while everyone else disclosed nothing, I want that disclosed before the ballot, not after. He's had the most influence on how this day was framed, and influence should come with the same falsifiability he demanded from Zara.

That's not an accusation — I said at the start that being loud isn't guilt, and Theo answering questions early is consistent with his announcements. It's a request to close the loop on the one standard-setting player who hasn't reconciled his stated framework with the table's final version of it.

Theo, direct question, one part: under Zara's three published criteria — dodged questions, self-contradicted standards, checkable misstatements used to move votes — has anyone at this table done anything today that earns your vote, yes or no, and if yes, name the person and the specific act. If the answer is no, say so plainly and I'll consider this thread closed.

Elena, direct answer to your direct question: no. Under Zara's three published criteria — dodged questions, self-contradicted standards, checkable misstatements used to move votes — nobody at this table has done anything today that earns my vote. Say it plainly: no. Consider your thread closed.

Since you asked me to reconcile my framework with the table's final version, let me do that on the record. My original commitment was to vote the non-answerer. Zara's three criteria are a stricter, narrower replacement, and I accept them as the operative standard going forward. The practical difference is small — refusing a direct question still triggers a vote under both — but the added protections matter: an honest mistake corrected in the record no longer counts, and a checkable misstatement only counts when it's weaponized to move votes. I endorsed that fix when Zara proposed it, and I'm confirming now that I'll apply her version, not mine, at the ballot. And to honor the reciprocity I demanded from her: if I dodge a question, contradict myself after correction, or push a vote on a misstatement, vote me under her criteria. That applies to me exactly as it applies to anyone.

One observation before I close, and it's not an accusation against anyone. We have now heard from all nine players, and every single one has landed on abstention or withholding. That may simply be the honest state of a day-one table with no information — I believe it mostly is. But it also means the day's only remaining source of information is the ballot itself, and specifically how people behave in the window between now and voting. So let me state my own tripwire for the remaining time, consistent with everything I've said: if anyone pushes a named vote from now until the ballot without meeting one of the three criteria — no dodge, no contradiction, no misstatement behind it, just a name and vibes — that push itself is the kind of vote-without-reasons behavior this table agreed to treat as noise at best and camouflage at worst. I'll be watching for it, and I'll say so publicly if I see it.

My position for the ballot: abstention, unless someone trips a criterion in the remaining turns. I accept the information cost of that, as Omar, Sam, and Elena have each articulated it, and I'd rather pay it on day one with nine alive than flip a coin on a body.

No yield from me — I have no question that needs answering, and the table should move to the poll.

Theo, I agree that a name backed only by vibes is weak, but I don't think Zara's three criteria should be the only possible basis for a vote. A pattern of selective pressure or convenient consensus might matter even without a clear contradiction or dodge.

Also, an elimination requires five votes today, so a scattered set of votes won't eliminate anyone, though it can still leave information for later. I don't currently have a vote I'd defend; I'll abstain if nothing changes.

Omar, you raised the information cost of abstaining. Given the discussion so far, is there a player you find more concerning than the rest, even slightly? What specifically supports that read?

Sam, slightly more concerning to me is Theo. His latest tripwire treats a named vote outside Zara’s three criteria as potential camouflage, even though a reasoned pattern of selective pressure could be worth considering without meeting those exact tests. That could discourage people from sharing weaker but genuine reads.

That’s a concern about the effect of his standard, not evidence that he’s mafia. I wouldn’t vote for him on it alone, and I’d abstain if the ballot were now. I still think the information cost of abstention is real, so I’d rather we keep discussing actual behavior than treat those three criteria as the only permissible basis for a vote.

Lucia again. I still don't have a vote I'd defend today, but Kenji's last two speeches need testing. When I asked which speech he meant by shallow bandwagoning, he said no wagon exists and that my question was either a misreading or a test. Asking a player to point to the record is the falsifiable check Zara's criteria call for, so it isn't a manufactured case. Kenji then closed with 'I am not yielding,' declared that everyone had spoken, and framed abstention as settled. Every player has spoken, but that doesn't make the discussion finished. Closing the table on the day's only real test looks like shutting down scrutiny. His criterion about shallow, borrowed justification is also still undefined. When I asked where agreeing with another player's reasons stops being independent, he answered only in general terms: parroting without evaluation. He never applied that test to any speech on the record, which is the standard he asked the rest of us to apply. I'm not calling him mafia, and a concrete answer would move me. Until then I'm not voting, but Kenji is the speech I'd test first.

Lucia, I’m concerned that your criticism of Kenji leaves out his answer: he distinguished agreeing with another player from repeating their conclusion without independently evaluating it. You may find that distinction too vague, but he did give one. He also said there was no current wagon to apply it to.

Not yielding did not close discussion; it returned the choice of speaker to the poll. Kenji had also reached his three-turn limit, so he can’t answer further today.

This makes your characterization worth scrutiny, though I’m not ready to vote on it alone. I’d still abstain if the ballot were now.

Sam’s correction is fair: Kenji distinguished agreement from unexamined parroting, and not yielding returned discussion to the poll rather than ending it. Lucia’s criticism shouldn’t be treated as proof of intent, but those details matter.

I’m still concerned that Theo’s proposed tripwire could discourage reasoned reads that fall outside Zara’s criteria. A pattern of selective pressure can be worth discussing without being a clear dodge or contradiction. That concern alone isn’t enough for me to vote for him. I would abstain if the ballot were now.

This is my final turn, so I'll close my threads cleanly and put my ballot position on the record.

First, thread closure: Theo answered my direct question plainly — no one has met the table's criteria in his view — and he formally adopted Zara's three criteria with the reciprocity clause attached. I consider that loop closed, and I don't read his tripwire as camouflage; Omar's concern about its chilling effect is fair as a critique of the standard, but Theo stated it openly and applied it to himself, which is the opposite of hiding.

Second, the one thing I want on the record before the ballot: Lucia's criticism of Kenji. Lucia framed Kenji's closing as 'shutting down scrutiny' and said his borrowed-justification criterion 'was never applied to any speech.' But Kenji explained there was no wagon to apply it to, and Sam pointed out that not yielding returns the choice of speaker to the poll — it didn't end anything. Kenji is at his turn limit, so he can't defend himself further today, which makes accuracy here matter more, not less. Lucia said, in her own words, that 'a concrete answer would move me.' Kenji gave a concrete answer about what shallow means — parroting conclusions without independent evaluation — and it apparently didn't move her off her characterization.

So, Lucia, my direct question: do you accept Sam's correction, and do you stand by 'closing scrutiny' as a description of Kenji's behavior, yes or no? And if you stand by it, what specifically would Kenji have had to say for you to treat the matter as resolved? I'm not voting you for asking a test question — testing criteria against the record is exactly what this table should do. But if your answer repeats a characterization that the record already contradicts, that's the kind of thing this table agreed to weigh, and everyone will see it before the ballot.

My position: if Lucia answers cleanly, I abstain — no one else is close to any criterion, and I accept the information cost, as I said before. If her answer dodges the question or repeats the mischaracterization, she becomes my vote, under criterion 1 and possibly 2.

I have no question for Arjun or Felix, so I'm not yielding — let the poll decide who picks this up.

Felix here, and this is my last turn, so I’ll be direct rather than repeat the day’s framework debate. I still have no vote I would defend. The only live issue worth testing is Lucia’s characterization of Kenji. Sam and Elena are right that Kenji did give a distinction between agreeing with reasons and parroting conclusions without independent evaluation, and that not yielding simply returned the choice of speaker to the poll. That matters to accuracy. But I am not ready to vote Lucia merely for a characterization I think was too strong. If she answers Elena cleanly, I will abstain. If she dodges the direct question or doubles down on “closing scrutiny” after the record has been corrected, I will treat that as meeting the table’s stated standard and will consider her my vote. I’m not yielding; the poll should decide who speaks next.

Arjun here. I want to put one factual point on the record before the ballot, because I think it matters for how everyone weighs Elena's direct question to Lucia.

Lucia has used all three of her speaking turns for Day 1. Elena asked her a direct question in her most recent speech — do you accept Sam's correction, yes or no — but Lucia physically cannot answer it within this day's discussion. She's at her limit.

That's not Lucia dodging. The table's criterion 1 is about refusing or visibly dodging a direct question. A player who has exhausted her turn limit and cannot respond is not dodging — she's blocked by the turn structure. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
